n: After the battle and his refusal of Sodom’s riches, Abram may have feared revenge or wondered about his reward. God comforts him in a vision: God Himself is Abram’s protection and his greatest reward.

f.g: The first “fear not” in the Bible, a phrase God often uses to comfort His servants.
Hebrew maḥazeh — something seen by revelation.

n: Abram honestly pours out his concern: what good are rewards if he has no child? His servant Eliezer of Damascus stands to inherit everything.
Abram repeats his worry. Ancient custom allowed a childless man to adopt a trusted servant as heir. Abram is not rebellious, just honest with God about his pain.

f.g: A servant born into his household.

n: God answers clearly: Abram’s heir will be his own son, not a servant.

f.g: From your own body—your biological child.

n: God takes Abram outside and shows him the night sky: “count the stars—so shall your descendants be.” The book of Abraham also records the Lord showing Abraham the stars and promising innumerable posterity.
Abram believes God, and God counts his faith as righteousness. Paul uses this verse as a key example of faith in God’s promises.

f.g: Credited or reckoned to his account.

n: God reminds Abram that He brought him out of Ur in order to give him this land. The book of Abraham tells how the Lord rescued him from idolatrous priests there.

f.w: brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees

n: Abram asks how he can know he will inherit the land. The JST adds that Abram saw the days of the Son of Man and rejoiced, learning that the promise looked forward to resurrection.

f.g: JST Genesis 15:9-12 adds that Abram saw the days of the Son of Man and believed.

n: God commands Abram to prepare animals for a covenant ceremony. These are the same kinds of animals later used in Israel’s sacrifices.
Abram cuts the animals in half and lays the halves opposite each other. In ancient covenants, parties would walk between the pieces, saying in effect, “May this happen to me if I break my word.”
Birds of prey swoop down on the carcasses, and Abram drives them away. Faith sometimes means guarding sacred things while waiting on God.

f.g: Birds of prey, such as vultures.

n: As the sun sets, Abram falls into a deep sleep, and a terrifying darkness comes over him—a sign of the hard times his descendants will face.

f.g: The same word used of Adam’s sleep in 2:21—a state for divine action and revelation.

n: God reveals that Abram’s descendants will be foreigners and slaves in another land for four hundred years. This foreshadows Israel’s bondage in Egypt.
God promises to judge the oppressing nation, and Israel will leave with great wealth—fulfilled in the Exodus.
Abram himself will die peacefully at a good old age. God’s promises are often fulfilled beyond a single lifetime.

f.g: An idiom for dying and joining one’s ancestors.

n: The delay is partly because the Amorites’ wickedness has not yet reached its full measure. God is patient even with the wicked, giving them time to repent before judgment.

f.w: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full

f.g: Probably long generations of about a century each.

n: In the darkness, a smoking firepot and a blazing torch pass between the pieces—representing God Himself. Only God walks through, showing He alone guarantees this covenant.

f.w: a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp
f.g: Fire and smoke often signal God’s presence, as in the pillar of fire and Sinai.

n: God formally “cuts” a covenant, promising the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates. This territory was most nearly reached in the days of David and Solomon.

f.g: Literally “cut a covenant,” fitting the ceremony.
Probably the Wadi el-Arish on Egypt’s border, or the Nile.

n: The peoples then living in the land are listed, beginning with lesser-known groups.

f.g: A people later friendly to Israel; Moses’ father-in-law was a Kenite (Judges 1:16).

n: The list continues with the Hittites, Perizzites, and Rephaim.
The list closes with the main peoples of Canaan, including the Jebusites of Jerusalem. Ten nations are named in all—a number suggesting completeness.
